It is immediately apparent from the composite map that far west reaches of the state are the most restrictive with regard to siting. Looking to the constituent layers below, this is due to a series of factors. The primary restrictions seem to be the series of steep mountain ranges, national forests, Native American reservations, and other protected regions that span from Glacier National Park in the northwest to Park and Sweet Grass counties near the northern edge of Yellowstone National Park. To a lesser extent, the active fault lines and associated seismic activity that can sometimes coincide with mountain ranges present additional barriers to siting. In contrast, the predominant barrier to siting in the eastern portion of Montana is access to cooling water, for which the large LWR has the greatest requirement. The combination of protected regions and mountain ranges in the west with limited streamflow in the east means that the vast majority of baseline suitable land in Montana is found in the riparian zones of the Missouri and Yellowstone Rivers. Consequently, the counties with the greatest amount of suitable land are Treasure (85.7%), Richland (75.5%), Chouteau (74.3%), Prairie (70.1%) and Hill (68.3%). In total, only 11 of Montana’s 56 counties exceed 50% suitability, with four having no suitable land: Carter, Daniels, Powder River, and Wheatland. These dynamics largely hold true for the small modular reactor siting results in Table M2. While the population, slope, and cooling water data layers have differing setbacks and thresholds from the large LWR, most of the meaningful changes take place in the western portion of the state. Consequently, the additional siting restrictions that do not change between technology configurations significantly limit the impact of the relaxed constraints in the small modular reactor siting regime. Looking to the raw percentages by county, however, it is immediately evident that many do gain some amount of suitable land. The most suitable counties gain between 5 and 10% of additional suitable land, with the exception of Prairie County, which is supplanted by Teton County at 72.9% suitability.
